comment: The baked APPROVED-MOD WHITELIST — mods a Dungeon Train run may have installed and still count.
Anything installed and NOT approved makes the session Free Play (once enforcement is on).
Every id here is a real modId as ModList.get().getMods() reports it, NOT a CurseForge/Modrinth
slug: Item Highlighter ships as `highlighter`, Iris Shaders as `iris`, Interactive Player Mobs
as `playermob`. An id transcribed from a store URL silently free-plays that mod's players, so
check the mod's own neoforge.mods.toml or the relay's Approved Mods page (which lists the ids
players actually report) before adding one.
This file is the OFFLINE fallback and the starting point. The relay serves approvals and
revocations on top of it (GET /<CAP>/approved-mods), so the live list is:
Curate here for things that should ship in the jar; curate on the relay for everything else.
THE RULE FOR ADDING SOMETHING: approve mods that change how the game LOOKS, SOUNDS, PERFORMS or
READS, and libraries that do nothing on their own. Do not approve mods that change what the game
GIVES you — loot, mobs, structures, recipes, progression, movement — however popular they are.
Those runs are not comparable to anyone else's, which is the whole reason Free Play exists.
Nothing here overrides the cheat-mod blacklist: a mod on both lists is still a cheat mod.
prefixesWhy: Sinytra Connector's Forgified Fabric API registers ~45 separate underscore-namespaced modules
(fabric_api_base, fabric_renderer_api_v1, ...) and ~98% of our players load them. They are
platform plumbing whose membership is Connector's to change, so a rule beats a transcription
that goes stale silently — the same call generateModRoster already makes in build.gradle.
Matched on the RAW id, so the underscore namespace is all that matches: a mod called
"Fabric Furniture" (modId fabricfurniture) is untouched. A prefix never beats a revocation:
an exact id revoked from the relay stays unapproved even if a prefix would have matched it.

platform.why: The game and the loader. Never optional, never a choice a player made.

dungeon_train.why: Dungeon Train itself, its required physics engine, and the mods we ship inside our own jar or as siblings. Every player has these.

modpack_roster.why: Every mod either modpack bundles (modpack/modpack.config.json optional_mods), whether it ships on by default or opt-in. Approving these is not a judgement call — we put them on the player's disk.
note: worldedit is here because the modpack ships it, not because it is harmless — it can build
anything from thin air. Its commands are not on CommandAllowlist, so USING it still taints
the run; only having it installed does not. Same use-not-presence split as Effortless

performance.why: Frame rate and memory only. They change nothing a player can get.

visual.why: How the game looks and animates. Cosmetic: no reach, no resources, no information a vanilla player lacks.
note: lambdynlights (dynamic lights from held torches) is a genuine borderline call — it lets you
see a little further into an unlit room. Approved because the alternative is a player
holding a torch, and because DT's difficulty comes from the train, not from darkness.
Revoke it from the relay if that stops being true.

interface.why: HUD, menus, tooltips, inventory handling and recipe viewers. They present what the game already tells you.

note: A deliberate call, not an oversight. A minimap shows terrain the player has already been
shown, and every one of these is near-standard equipment. Their entity radar / cave layers
are the part that would be an advantage — revoke a specific mod from the relay if that
starts mattering rather than pre-emptively free-playing everyone who runs a map.

multiplayer.why: Playing with other people: hosting, cosmetics and social layers.

libraries.why: Do nothing on their own — they arrive as a dependency of something else, and that something else still has to be approved in its own right. Approving the library layer costs nothing and stops a player being free-played by their mod's plumbing.
